title: Game 11: Magnus vs Hans
notes: Game 11 of 12 in the experiment, from the Queen's Gambit Declined. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.

This is a standard Queen's Gambit Declined; I just complete my development solidly with e3, supporting d4 and opening the f1-bishop's diagonal while keeping the Bg5 pin on f6. No enemy captures or checks are available, and nothing of mine is loose.

This is the Orthodox Queen's Gambit Declined, and the natural developing move is to castle, after which I'll follow up with Nbd7 and c6 or an h6/dxc4 freeing plan. I checked that castling costs nothing tactically: 6.cxd5 exd5 is comfortable, and nothing hits my kingside since the Bg5 is already pinned to nothing and e5 isn't available to White.

This is the standard QGD Classical; 6.Nxd5 exd5 7.cxd5 Nxd5 just trades off and relieves Black, so I develop with the main line 6.Nf3, completing my kingside development and keeping d4 well supported by e3, Nf3 and the queen. No loose pieces: Bg5 is protected by the pin-pressure after any ...Ne4 (Bxe7 Qxe7), and Black has no checks or captures that win material.

This is the Orthodox QGD; I want to resolve the Bg5 pin on my terms, and 6...h6 asks the bishop to decide — 7.Bh4 lets me continue with the Tartakower ...b6 and ...Bb7, while 7.Bxf6 Bxf6 gives me a comfortable dark-squared bishop and easy development. I checked that there's no tactic against h6 since nothing of mine hangs and g5 ideas are impossible for White here.

Black's ...h6 questions my bishop, so I retreat along the diagonal to h4, keeping the pin-pressure on f6 and avoiding the trade that would hand Black a strong dark-squared bishop; Bxf6 Bxf6 eases Black's game, while Bh4 keeps tension and all my pieces defended (no checks or captures available to Black after it).

This is a QGD where White's bishop has retreated to h4, so I want to complete development with a Tartakower-style setup. 7...b6 prepares ...Bb7 and ...c5 while keeping my structure solid; I checked that cxd5 exd5 or Qc2 give White nothing immediate, and tactical tries like ...Ne4 only help White after Bxe7 and Nd2 hitting the loose pawn.

I checked Nxd5 first: 8.Nxd5 exd5 9.cxd5 Nxd5 just loses a piece for two pawns, so the d5 pawn is poisoned. Instead I take with the pawn to reach a favourable Carlsbad structure — after 8.cxd5 exd5 Black's ...b6 has weakened the queenside and my minority attack with b4/Rc1 plus the Bh4/Nf3 setup gives me a comfortable edge, and nothing of mine is loose or hit by a check.

White's cxd5 must be answered; exd5 keeps a solid symmetrical structure and lets my bishop come to b7, while Nxd5 would invite Nxd5 and Bxe7 trades that loosen my kingside. After exd5 Bxf6 Bxf6 I'm perfectly comfortable.

I checked Nxd5 and Bxf6 first — the "pin" on f6 is fake since e7 is defended twice, so Nxd5 Nxd5 just drops a piece, and Bxf6 Bxf6 Nxd5 Bxd4 also loses a knight for pawns. Instead I develop with Bd3 in the standard Exchange QGD setup, aiming for O-O, Qc2 and Rab1 with a minority attack; Bd3 is attacked by nothing and leaves no piece loose.

I want to complete development naturally in this Exchange QGD structure; Bb7 puts the bishop on its best diagonal, supports a later c5 or Ne4 ideas, and keeps d5 well guarded (if Bxf6 Bxf6, Nxd5 just loses a piece to Bxd5). Lines like 9...Ne4 fail to 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Nxe4 dxe4 12.Bxe4 dropping a pawn.

The tempting 10.Nxd5 just loses a piece (10...Nxd5 and after Bxe7 Qxe7 I'm a knight for a pawn down), so I complete development instead; castling removes my king from the e-file before opening lines and prepares Qc2/Rab1 with the minority attack. Black has no checks or captures that hit anything loose after O-O.

The symmetrical structure invites simplification, and Ne4 is securely supported by Bb7 along the b7-e4 diagonal — if White tries Nxe4 dxe4 Bxe4, then Bxe4 just wins a piece. After the likely 11.Bxe7 Qxe7 12.Qc2 Nxc3, I relieve the pressure and reach a comfortable, solid position.

I checked the tempting captures first: 11.Nxe4 dxe4 forks my Bd3 and Nf3, and 11.Nxd5/Bxe4 lines end up giving a bishop for a pawn after the full recapture chain on e4, so both are out; 11.Ne5 even drops Bh4 since it unguards it. Instead I trade off Black's only well-placed defender with 11.Bxe7 Qxe7 (the sole recapture), after which Nc3 and Bd3 both hit the unsupported-by-pieces Ne4 and I can follow with Qc2 or Rc1 against Black's undeveloped queenside.

I must recapture the bishop, and Qxe7 is the natural Lasker-style move, keeping my strong knight on e4 and good development. I checked Nxe4 dxe4 Bxe4 Bxe4, where White's bishop on e4 is undefended after the knight leaves f3, so that line just loses material for White; other trades like Nxd5 Bxd5 are harmless equal exchanges.

Black's Ne4 is unsupported by pawns, so I eliminate it: 12.Bxe4 forces 12...dxe4 (12...Bxe4 13.Nxe4 dxe4 14.Nd2 just drops the pawn), and after 13.Nd2 the e4 pawn is attacked twice and defended once, so Black must weaken himself with ...f5 while his Bb7 is entombed behind the e4 pawn. The recapture dxe4 only hits my Nf3, which happily relocates to d2 with tempo, and opens nothing toward my king.

Qxe4 simply loses the queen since the bishop on e4 is defended by the knight on c3, so I must recapture with the pawn. dxe4 gains a tempo by hitting the f3 knight, and after Nd2 or Ne5 my bishop on b7 (reinforced by f5 if needed) holds the e4 wedge while I develop with Nc6 and the rooks.

I counted the capture chain on e4: immediate 13.Nxe4?? Bxe4 just drops a piece since nothing of mine guards e4, so I first add a second attacker with Nd2, after which Ndxe4 or f3 breaking up the e4 pawn both regain my material with a healthier structure. Nd2 also keeps everything guarded (Nc3 by b2, d4/e3 covered) and Black has no checks or counter-captures.

My e4 pawn is attacked twice by the knights, so I need support: Bd5 defends it and plants the bishop on a strong central square, since 14.Ncxe4 Bxe4 15.Ndxe4 Qxe4 would trade two knights for bishop and pawn in my favour. It's more active than the passive 13...f5.

Black's 13...Bd5 placed the bishop on a square attacked by my Nc3 and defended by nothing — no c6/e6 pawn, and the queen on e7 doesn't cover d5 (her diagonals run d8/f8/d6/f6). I checked the alternative Ncxe4, but after Bxe4 Nxe4 Qxe4 the e-file queen wins my knight back, so instead I simply take the undefended bishop; after Nxd5 Black has no checks or captures on my loose pieces.

My queen on e7 is attacked by the knight that just landed on d5, so I must move it, and I'm already a piece down after the Bd5 blunder, so I want maximum activity. Qd6 steps off the knight's attack while hitting the undefended knight on d5, guarding c7, and adding pressure to d4 (Nxc7 or Nxb6 fail to Qxc7 and axb6).

My Nd5 is attacked by Qd6 and undefended, but 15.Nxe4 grabs the pawn and simultaneously attacks the queen, so Black has no time to just win the d5 knight. I checked the tries: 15...Qxd5 16.Nf6+! gxf6 (Rxf6 is impossible, f7 blocks) 17.Qxd5 wins the queen; 15...Qe6/Qe5 double-attacking both knights is met by 16.Nc3, which saves the d5 knight and defends e4; and 15...f5 simply loses the queen to 16.Nxd6.

White's Nxe4 attacks my queen on d6, but it leaves the knight on d5 completely undefended — the d4 pawn doesn't cover d5 and nothing else does either. Qxd5 both saves my queen and wins a piece; the only try, Nf6+, just loses the knight to gxf6.

My Ne4 is attacked by Qd5 and completely undefended, and I'm a clean pawn up, so I must save it with tempo: Nc3 hits the queen and is protected by the b2 pawn, while opening the d-file so Qxd4 is impossible (Qd1 guards d4). Nc5/Nd6/Nf6+/Ng5 all drop the knight to a capture, and Nc3 keeps the extra pawn with a solid structure.

Qxa2 and Qxd4 both lose the queen (Ra1 and Qd1 cover those squares), and Qxg2+ is simply met by Kxg2, so I need normal development. Nc6 brings my last piece out while hitting the d4 pawn, and if White tries Nb5 I get counterplay with Nxd4 liquidating into an equal ending.
Black's 16...Nc6 ignored that my knight on c3 already attacks d5, and I verified d5 is defended by nothing — the knight on c6 covers d4/e5/b4 but not d5, no pawn or rook reaches it.

I'm down a queen for a knight after the blunder on move 16, so I just need to consolidate: Nxd4 drops the knight (the queen defends d4 through the pinned file), Ne7 and Nb4 lose the knight outright, and any rook on d8 allows Nxc7 hitting a8. Rac8 defends c7, keeps b6 covered by a7/c7, and prepares Rfd8 to challenge the knight.

I'm up a queen for a knight, so the priority is safety and simplification, not grabbing pawns: Nxb6 and Nxc7 both just lose the knight to cxb6/Rxc7, and Ne7+/Nf6+ drop it to Nxe7 or gxf6. Rc1 contests the open file and offers a one-for-one rook trade (Rxc1 Qxc1 or Rxc1), while d4 stays guarded by my queen if ...Nxd4 is tried.

My knight on c6 is hanging to Rxc6 (the c7 pawn blocks my rook), so I need counterplay rather than a passive retreat — and I noticed White's Nd5 is actually undefended, since the d4 pawn blocks the queen on d1. Rfd8 hits that knight, so Rxc6 allows Rxd5 with an even trade, and Ne7+ is simply met by Nxe7.

I'm up a full queen for nothing, so I want safe simplification: Nb4 would actually just drop the knight since nothing recaptures on b4, but Nxc7 is sound because the knight is defended by Rc1, so 19...Rxc7 20.Rxc7 nets a clean pawn and trades a pair of rooks. Black's counter ...Nxd4/...Rxd4 fails since my Qd1 guards d4 and wins the recapturing piece.

I'm already down a queen for a bishop after the earlier tactic, so I must at least win back the forked knight on c7. Rxc7 regains the piece; after 20.Rxc7 Nxd4 21.exd4 Rxd4 I keep a rook and four pawns and still have a fighting chance to build a fortress.

I'm up a queen for a knight, so I want to keep everything safe while gaining tempo: d5 kicks the Nc6 off its post (it was the only piece pressuring d4), and the pawn is immune since Rxd5 simply loses the rook to Qxd5. Once the knight steps away the c-file opens and Rxc7 wins the undefended rook, and Black has no checks or captures in reply.

My rook on c7 is hanging to Rc1 and my knight on c6 is attacked by the d5 pawn, so I need a move that handles both — Rcc8 keeps the rook safe (defended by Rd8) while the rook on c8 now guards the knight on c6. It also keeps my other rook on the d-file opposing the queen, so 21.Rxc6 Rxd1 22.Rxd1 Rxc6 or 21.dxc6 Rxd1 wins the queen back for a rook; moving the knight instead would simply drop the rook.

Counting the capture chain on c6: the knight is defended only by Rc8, so 21.dxc6 Rxc6 leaves that rook loose, and I can follow with Qa4 or Rxc6 — either way I win the knight outright and stay a queen plus pawns ahead. I checked Black has no checks or counter-captures (my king's pawn shield is intact and Rxd1 just gives up both rooks for the queen), so this simple capture is safe.

I'm already down a queen after an earlier blunder, but the d-file is wide open and White's queen on d1 sits right in front of my rook — Rxd1 wins the queen for a rook, which is the best practical exchange available. After 22.Rfxd1 I still face the strong c6 pawn, but trading rook for queen is clearly the least bad option; grabbing c6 instead just loses a rook to Rxc6.

Black's rook on d1 is attacked twice and completely undefended (his Rc8 is blocked by my own c6 pawn and my Rc1), so I simply win a full rook. I take with the f1 rook so that Rc1 keeps guarding the c6 passer — after Rcxd1 instead, ...Rxc6 would snatch the pawn for free.

I'm already a rook down, and Rxc6 just loses my last rook since the c-pawn is defended by Rc1, so I must keep the rook on c8 to block the passer. Kf8 brings my king toward the c-file to help contain the pawn without weakening my position further.

I'm a full rook up, so I want a forcing move that doesn't let the extra rook evaporate: 23.Rd8+ either wins the c8 rook outright after 23...Ke7 24.Rxc8, or after 23...Rxd8 24.c7 the pawn forks the rook, forcing 24...Rc8 where Black's rook is paralyzed forever and my king walks in to eat the queenside. I keep Rc1 guarding c7 and avoid any premature rook trade into a pure pawn race.

Ke7 just loses a rook since Rxc8 is defended by the rook on c1, so the capture is forced. After Rxd8 I keep material level in rooks and can fight the advanced c-pawn with Rd7 or Rc8, keeping the rook behind/in front of the passer.

I'm up two pawns with a far-advanced passer, so instead of offering a rook trade with Rd1 (which my Game 8 mistake warns against — simplifying into a pawn race) I push 24.c7, hitting the rook: Rd7 allows 25.c8=Q+, so Black must play Rc8 where my Rc1 defends the pawn and his rook is paralysed forever while my king and kingside pawns advance.

The c7 pawn threatens to promote, and leaving the rook on d8 just loses it to c8=Q Rxc8 Rxc8+, while Rd1+ allows Rxd1; king moves lose the same way. Rc8 blockades the promotion square and is immune from Rxc8 because White's own c7 pawn blocks the file, after which I can bring my king via e7-d7 to help win that pawn.

Black's rook on c8 is completely frozen by my c7 pawn (any move allows c8=Q, and Rxc7 loses to Rxc7), but his king is heading for d7/b7 to cover c8 and free the rook, so I must cash in now. Rc6 keeps c7 defended, is attacked by nothing (the b6 pawn hits a5/c5, the c8 rook is blocked by my own pawn), and wins the undefended b6 pawn; even after ...Kd7 Rxb6 Kxc7 I'm two clean pawns up with the far more active rook and his king stranded on the queenside.

My rook is chained to c8 to stop the c7 pawn, and Rxc7 just drops the rook to Rxc7 since the pawn is defended by the rook on c6. My only real counterplay is to march the king over to attack the c7 pawn, so Ke7 heading for d7 is the move.

Every rook move off the c-file loses material — Re6+ and Rf6/Rd6 run into Kx (the king on e7 touches those squares), Rg6 into fxg6, Rxb6 into axb6 and Rxh6 into gxh6 — so I must keep the rook on c6 where it holds my c7 pawn and freezes Black's rook on c8. With Black's rook paralysed I improve on the queenside: a4-a5 will undermine b6 (after axb6 axb6 the pawn falls to my rook), and my king can walk up later.

I'm two pawns down with my rook chained to c8 by the c7 pawn, so I must activate my king: Kd7 attacks the loose rook on c6 and threatens to win the pawn (if White keeps the rook on the c-file, Rxc7 Rxc7+ Kxc7 liquidates into a pawn ending only one pawn down). White's best is probably Rxb6 Rxc7, but at least then my rook is free and my king is central.

My rook on c6 is attacked by Kd7 and undefended, so I must move it but keep it on the c-file to guard my monster c7 pawn (Rxb6 axb6 and Rxh6 gxh6 both drop the rook — recount defenders!). Rc3 is protected by the b2 pawn, so Black's king can never harass it, it holds c7, and it frees me to march Kf1-e2-d3-e4 so that if Black ever liquidates with ...Rxc7 Rxc7+ Kxc7 I meet the 6v5 pawn ending with a dominant central king and a kingside majority.

The c7 pawn is attacked twice (rook and king) and only defended once, so Rxc7 Rxc7+ Kxc7 wins a pawn and liquidates the rooks, which is much better than leaving my rook passively glued to c8 while White's king marches up. The resulting king-and-pawn ending leaves me only one pawn down (4v3 kingside, 2v2 queenside) with my king close enough to run to e5 and defend.

My rook on c3 is only safe there because b2 guards it — every other c-file square (Rc1/Rc2/Rc4/Rc5/Rc6) just drops the rook to Rxc-something, so the real choice is Rxc7+ or stepping off the file with tempo. Remembering Game 8, I don't want to liquidate my extra pawn into a pure pawn endgame where Black's king on c7 is far more central than mine on g1; instead Rd3+ gains a tempo, drives the king, and lets me follow with Rd4 (covering a4 and b2 on the fourth rank) plus Kf1-e2 to march my king up with the extra pawn intact.

I'm a pawn down in a rook endgame, and White's extra pawn lies in the kingside majority (e,f,g,h vs f,g,h), so my king must head that way rather than to the balanced queenside. Ke6 centralizes actively, blockades the extra pawn's advance, and keeps my rook free to invade via c2; Kc6 would be too passive on the side where pawns are equal, and the retreats Kc8/Ke8 just lose time.

I'm a clean pawn up in a rook endgame, so I must keep my rook active and avoid trading into a pawn ending where Black's centralized king would outrun mine (Rd2 is too passive, Rd5/Rd6+/Rd7 simply drop the rook to Kxd5/Kxd6/Rxd7). Rd4 centralizes, guards a4 along the fourth rank, stops ...Rc4, and after ...Rc1+ Kh2 ...Rc2 I have Rb4 defending b2 while hitting b6.

I'm a pawn down in a rook ending, so activity is my main resource; Rc2 grabs the second rank, hits the loose b2 pawn and prepares Rc4 to harass a4. If White answers Rd2 I decline the trade with Rc4, and attempts like Re4+ just lose the rook to Kd5/Kf5.

My b2 pawn is loose and Rd2 or Rc4 would simply lose the rook, since the rook cannot defend the square it moves to (my old Rf5/Rxe5 mistake). Rb4 defends b2 along the file while attacking the weak b6 pawn, keeping my extra pawn and the more active rook.

The white king on g1 is boxed in by its own pawns on f2, g2, h2, so the back rank is the only escape — and my rook can seize it. Rc1 delivers checkmate since f1 and h1 are covered along the first rank and no white piece can capture or block.

new_lessons: [endgame] In rook endings, before every rook move ask if an enemy rook can land on your back rank; if your king sits behind untouched f2-g2-h2, play h3/g3 or Kf1 first Example: 29.Rd4?? Rc1+ 30.Rd1 Rxd1 mate, 56%→2%

[endgame] When your rook can take an enemy rook with check, take it; fear of a "worse pawn race" never justifies declining a capture with check while material up Example: 28.Rd3+ instead of 28.Rxc7+ threw away 82%→54%

[endgame] Once an enemy rook reaches your second rank, answer with opposition on that rank (Rd2/Rd1) or Kh2 luft; do not drift sideways to guard a pawn Example: 30.Rb4?? "defending b2" allowed 30...Rc1 mate

[middlegame] Before every move, list enemy checks and captures, your loose pieces, and each bishop/rook/knight line hitting your destination square; if one wins material, choose otherwise Example: 13...Qc7?? Bxc7 (Bf4 guarded c7); 11.Bc4?? Qh4+ then Qxc4

[middlegame] Play each capture chain to the end, recounting attackers and defenders after every trade; a piece never defends the square it moves to Example: ...Qc3 "forked" rooks but bxc3 won the queen; 27...Rf5 was defended by the rook that moved

[middlegame] When a piece is attacked, consider pawn moves that counterattack or gain tempo, and test whether the opponent has a check that removes your retreat square Example: 25...Nd6? lost to 26.Qg5+ Kh7 27.Qxf6 then Qxd6; 25...c5 held

[middlegame] Before trading a minor piece, play out the recapture: if a pawn recapture opens a file or diagonal to your king or leaves pawns loose, keep the piece Example: 17...Nc4 18.Bxc4 dxc4 opened the e-file for Re4 and left c4 hanging, 51%→9%

[middlegame] Keep a piece on an advanced square only if a pawn can support it; retreat it before enemy pawns remove every escape square Example: Unsupported Ne4 had no retreat after e5/d6; Bd5 and Be4 were chased by pawns

[middlegame] Never push pawns in front of your castled king while an enemy bishop or queen eyes those squares; meet a wing storm with a central break Example: 17.g3 invited ...fxg3 and ...Bxh3; 17.dxc6 kept a winning game

[middlegame] When your rook can invade the enemy second rank hitting loose pawns, prefer that to any equal trade; with exposed kings, activity beats simplification Example: Instead of 17...Nc4, 17...Rf2 grabbing h2 and tying White down was winning

[endgame] With extra material and rooks on an open file, do not offer a trade to a defended enemy rook; insert a check first, then keep both rooks active Example: 34...Re2 allowed 35.Rxe2; 34...Re1+ drove the king back, 98% vs 91%

[endgame] With extra material, trade one-for-one but never your last extra piece; cut off his king, take the seventh rank, push a passer only with escort Example: Refusing 31.Rd5 dropped 94%→61%; 59...b5 pushed an unescorted pawn

[endgame] Keep extra pawns connected, stay inside the square of every passer, and before each move check enemy Kx-captures and stalemate tricks Example: 66...Qc3+? Kxc3 drew a won queen endgame; 29...dxc4 scattered a6/c4/c6

[opening] Delay the central break (d5/e5) until minors are developed and the king is castled; when two units can recapture, use the minor piece, not the queen Example: 8...d5 exd5 left a backward pawn; 10...Qxd5? 11.Qxd5 lost a tempo

[middlegame] When a bishop pins your knight against king or a loose rook, kick the pinner with a3/h3 or block with Bd2 instead of defending passively with the queen Example: 12.Qd2 let ...Nc5-e4 pile on; 12.a3 questioned Bb4 at once
